passage:
Tuesday. Kunal's query crashed for the fourth time, and the error message might as well have been in Latin. Across the desk, Sonali finished her report in twenty minutes. "I can't do SQL," he muttered, and felt a hot little flash of resentment when she offered to look.
Thursday. He typed the same sentence into his notes, stopped, and added one word: "I can't do joins yet." Then, under it: "What do I try next?" He had spent two evenings rereading the same tutorial. That clearly wasn't working. So he asked Sonali for the smallest broken example she could think of.
The following Monday. Kunal wrote a join on a table of five rows, then fifty, then the real one. It ran. He still needed Sonali's help with the date filter, but this time he asked without the heat in his chest.

qa.q: What did Kunal add to his notes on Thursday?
qa.a: He added one word, "I can't do joins yet," and then wrote "What do I try next?"

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling on Tuesday when Sonali offered to look?
qa.a: He felt a hot flash of resentment, probably ashamed that she finished in twenty minutes while he kept failing.

qa.q: Which change in Kunal's approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Swapping rereading the same tutorial for small broken examples worked, because it gave him a new strategy instead of more of the same effort.

qa.q: How might Sonali experience the change in Kunal between Tuesday and Monday?
qa.a: On Tuesday Sonali may have felt shut out, but by Monday Kunal asks openly, so helping him probably feels easier and more welcome.

grounding: An adult reframes "I can't" into "I can't yet", asks what to try next, and changes strategy rather than only trying harder.

passage:
The new posters went up in the support centre on Monday: "Every mistake is a lesson!" Gurpreet, the shift manager, watched Nilesh walk under one at 8:58 and log straight into a queue of forty tickets.
By lunch he had escalated three calls he could probably have solved. When she asked why, he said, "If I get it wrong, it goes on my score. There's no time to try things."
She checked. The quality team marked every error, and nobody had given Nilesh a single piece of feedback in six weeks. His only training had been a video.
Gurpreet looked at the poster, then at his queue. That afternoon she blocked thirty minutes each day for him to shadow Ravi, and asked quality to hold his first month of scores as practice. The poster stayed up, but now it had something behind it.

qa.q: How many tickets were in Nilesh's queue when he logged in?
qa.a: He logged straight into a queue of forty tickets.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling as she looked from the poster to Nilesh's queue?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and a bit frustrated, seeing that the slogan asked for learning while nothing in Nilesh's day made learning safe.

qa.q: What could other managers take from Gurpreet's choice?
qa.a: They could back growth talk with time, feedback and safety, like daily shadowing and treating early scores as practice.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see the posters before Gurpreet's changes?
qa.a: He probably saw them as empty or even unfair, since every mistake still hurt his score and nobody had time to teach him.

grounding: A manager notices that growth slogans mean little without time, feedback and safety to learn, and adds that support.

subtype: Feeling like a fraud in a top college [Actor]
passage:
Hostel mentor's note, end of first semester, winter break week.
Simran came to my office the evening before most students left for home. The corridor was cold and half empty. She had topped her lab course, but she said, "They made a mistake admitting me. My entrance rank was near the cut-off. Everyone else here actually belongs."
I asked about the lab result. "Rajni helped me revise, so it doesn't count." When I mentioned her project grade, she shrugged: "Easy topic."
She compared herself only with the strongest students in her batch. She kept checking the door, as if someone might come in and agree with her.
What I did next: I asked her to write down three things she did herself this term and read them aloud. She managed two. I booked a follow-up for the first week back and gave her the counselling centre's number.

qa.q: Which course had Simran topped?
qa.a: She had topped her lab course.

qa.q: What does Simran checking the door suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels anxious and exposed, as if she expects to be found out at any moment.

qa.q: What small step helped Simran start to see her own part?
qa.a: Writing down three things she did herself and reading them aloud made her name her own effort, even though she managed only two.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel if she heard Simran say the lab result doesn't count?
qa.a: Rajni might feel sad or puzzled, since she knows revising together does not cancel the work Simran put in.

grounding: A student at a top college believes she got in by luck, dismisses each success and compares herself harshly with the best.

passage:
13 January, Lohri night
Everyone in the hostel lit a small fire on the terrace. I stood at the edge because I didn't know the songs, and honestly, I don't know half the words people use here either. "Office hours." "Elective pool." Someone asked what my parents do and I said "farming" too quietly.
I have 8.4 this semester. On paper I'm fine. So why do I feel like a guest who'll be asked to leave?
Then Rafiq, the third-year from the maths club, handed me a revri and said, "Baljeet, first time I heard 'office hours' I thought it meant the admin block." He's the first in his family at college too. He says there's a group of us who meet on Sundays and swap what nobody explains.
Going this Sunday. Feels less like I'm faking it tonight.

qa.q: What grade did Baljeet have that semester?
qa.a: Baljeet had 8.4 this semester.

qa.q: Why does Baljeet feel like a guest despite good marks?
qa.a: Baljeet feels out of place and unsure of belonging, because words like "office hours" and the terrace songs are unfamiliar, not because the work is too hard.

qa.q: What would you advise Baljeet about the Sunday group?
qa.a: Going is a good idea, since people there can explain the unwritten codes, and asking about unfamiliar words there costs nothing.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see Baljeet standing at the edge of the fire?
qa.a: Rafiq likely recognises his own first year in it, which is why he shares the office hours story to show Baljeet is not alone.

grounding: A first-generation student with good marks doubts belonging because college codes are unfamiliar, and a peer community eases it.

subtype: Working overly hard to avoid exposure [Actor]
passage:
During Diwali week the office emptied by six, sweets boxes stacked in the pantry, strings of lights blinking on the reception desk. Sarita stayed until ten again.
She had a ten-minute update in tomorrow's client call. She had written a script, then a backup script, then answers to twenty questions nobody was likely to ask.
Kamal stopped by with his coat on. "It's one slide, Sarita. You know this."
"If I miss something, they'll realise I shouldn't be here," she said, not looking up.
Next morning the call went well. The client thanked her. On the metro home she felt her shoulders drop, then thought, Only because I stayed till ten. If I hadn't, they'd have seen through me.
That night she opened the laptop to start preparing for Friday's call, which was still three days away.

qa.q: Until what time did Sarita stay at the office?
qa.a: Sarita stayed until ten again.

qa.q: What does Sarita feel on the metro home, and why does it not last?
qa.a: She feels relieved as her shoulders drop, but the relief turns back into fear because she credits the good call to staying late, not to her ability.

qa.q: What could Sarita try before Friday's call?
qa.a: She could prepare for a set time only and then stop, so she can see that she does well without the extra hours.

qa.q: What is it like for Kamal to watch Sarita every evening?
qa.a: Kamal probably feels concerned and a bit helpless, since he can see she knows her work but his reassurance doesn't reach her.

grounding: A new employee over-prepares out of fear of exposure, and each success credited to overwork keeps the fear going.

passage:
Sit down, sit down. You're wondering whether to recommend someone quiet for the lead role? Let me tell you about Jahnavi.
When I was a young engineer, just Kiran from the testing floor, Jahnavi sat two desks away. She found the bugs nobody else could. But in meetings she said nothing, and twice she turned down the team lead post. People thought she didn't care.
I watched her for months. One day, after she refused the promotion again, I stayed back and told her plainly: "The release didn't fail last spring because you caught the memory leak. Three of us learned testing from your notes. That is what you bring." She went red and said nothing. A week later she asked me to sit in on her first meeting as lead. So, my dear, tell your quiet one what they actually do. Be specific.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi turn down twice?
qa.a: She turned down the team lead post twice.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while watching Jahnavi stay silent and refuse promotions?
qa.a: Kiran felt admiring and a little concerned, watching her for months and then naming the memory leak and her notes instead of giving vague praise.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Jahnavi accept the lead role?
qa.a: The turning point was Kiran staying back and telling her exactly what her work had done, which seemed to give her the confidence to say yes.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have felt when she went red and said nothing?
qa.a: Jahnavi might have felt embarrassed but also seen and moved, since someone had finally noticed the value she brought.

grounding: A team member notices a skilled colleague who stays silent and refuses promotion, and tells her specifically what value she brings.

passage:
The ferry to Almada was nearly empty on a wet Thursday. Gabriel had been rehearsing the sentence since the morning stand-up.
"Tomas, can I tell you something stupid?" He watched the river instead of his mentor. "I think I'm a fraud. Every sprint I'm waiting for someone to notice I don't know what I'm doing."
Tomas laughed, not unkindly. "Stupid? I felt that for my first four years. Some weeks I still do." He counted on his fingers. "Ana felt it. Our CTO told me she felt it after her second promotion."
Gabriel turned. "Seriously?"
"Seriously. It usually means you care and you can see how much there is to know. It doesn't mean you're bad."
Gabriel let out a long breath. The sentence he had carried all day seemed lighter now, just something people said on ferries.

qa.q: Where were Gabriel and Tomas when Gabriel told his secret?
qa.a: They were on the ferry to Almada on a wet Thursday.

qa.q: Why does Gabriel watch the river instead of his mentor as he speaks?
qa.a: He feels ashamed and nervous about admitting he feels like a fraud, so looking away makes the confession easier.

qa.q: What went well in how Tomas responded?
qa.a: Tomas shared his own experience and named others who felt the same, which made the feeling normal and eased Gabriel's shame.

qa.q: How might Tomas see Gabriel after the ferry talk?
qa.a: Tomas probably sees Gabriel as someone who cares and is growing, not as a fraud, and may feel glad he was trusted with it.

grounding: An adult tells a mentor he feels like a fraud and learns that capable people feel the same, which eases his shame.

passage:
The summer holidays had just begun, and the colony park in Lucknow smelled of mango peels. Noor sat on the swing with her report card folded small in her pocket.
"Will you show your ammi the maths mark?" asked Payal.
"Not the maths." Noor had got fifteen out of twenty-five. Last time she'd got twenty-four, and Ammi had hugged her and cooked sevaiyan. When Noor had got eighteen in science, Ammi had only said, "Next time better," and gone to the kitchen without a hug.
"I'll say they're not out yet," Noor said. She pushed the swing higher so Payal wouldn't see her face.
That evening she quietly tore the maths page out of her rough book too, the one with the red crosses.

qa.q: What mark did Noor get in maths?
qa.a: Noor had got fifteen out of twenty-five.

qa.q: Why does Noor want to hide the maths mark from Ammi?
qa.a: She is worried and sad, because she remembers hugs and sevaiyan after a high mark and no hug after a lower one, so love seems to depend on marks.

qa.q: How could Ammi support Noor better?
qa.a: Ammi could show warmth whatever the mark, for example a hug first and then a calm talk about the red crosses, so mistakes feel safe to share.

qa.q: What might Payal think when Noor pushes the swing higher?
qa.a: Payal may sense Noor is upset and hiding something, and feel unsure whether to ask again.

grounding: A child whose mother warms only to high marks hides a poor result, feeling loved for performance.

passage:
Winter fog lay over the fields outside the kasba school, and the classroom windows were grey by four. The history notebook was due tomorrow.
Eshaan had begun his answer on the Mauryan empire nine times. Each time a letter leaned the wrong way, or a line ran crooked, he rubbed it out. The paper had gone thin and grey in the middle.
"Just write it, yaar," Sarika said from the next bench. "Sir only checks if it's there."
"It has to be right." He pressed the eraser again and the page split with a soft rip. He stared at the hole.
The next day, when Sir collected notebooks, Eshaan's page was empty except for the torn patch. He said he had forgotten it at home. It felt easier than handing in something he'd have hated.

qa.q: How many times had Eshaan begun his answer on the Mauryan empire?
qa.a: He had begun it nine times.

qa.q: Why does Eshaan say he forgot the notebook instead of handing in what he had?
qa.a: He feels ashamed and stuck, because anything less than perfect feels like failing, so handing in nothing seems less painful.

qa.q: What small step could help Eshaan next time?
qa.a: He could set a rule to write a full rough draft without erasing, then fix only one or two things before handing it in.

qa.q: If you were Sarika, what would you want Eshaan to know?
qa.a: Sarika would probably want him to know that a messy, finished answer is better than an empty page, and that she was worried watching him tear it.

grounding: A teenager erases and rewrites until the page tears and hands in nothing, because an imperfect answer feels like failure.

passage:
Copenhagen was dark by half past three that December, and the student kitchen smelled of Omar's mulled juice. Emil sat at the table with his thesis draft and a red pen.
"You got a twelve on every exam since first year," Omar said. "Why are you rewriting the introduction again?"
"Because they expect it now." Emil's pen hovered. "If this is just okay, everyone will see I was never special. I was just careful."
"Do you even like the topic?"
Emil paused. He used to. In second year he'd stayed up reading about harbour cities for fun. Now he mostly felt his stomach tighten when he opened the file.
"I'll like it when it's perfect," he said, and crossed out a sentence that had been fine.
Omar pushed a mug toward him and said nothing.

qa.q: What grade had Emil got on every exam since first year?
qa.a: He had got a twelve on every exam since first year.

qa.q: What is Emil afraid of as he keeps rewriting the introduction?
qa.a: He is afraid that any ordinary draft will show he was never special, so fear, more than love of the topic, is pushing him.

qa.q: What could Emil try to reconnect with why he chose this work?
qa.a: He could spend a little time reading about harbour cities just for interest again, and set a clear point where the introduction counts as done.

qa.q: How might Omar feel as he pushes the mug toward Emil and stays quiet?
qa.a: Omar is probably worried and caring, unsure how to help a friend who can't enjoy work he used to love.

grounding: A student praised for flawless work fears any mistake will expose him as ordinary, so fear now fuels his striving.
